H1.text: A suitcase on wheels glides with one finger. A steel cupboard, just as heavy, needs two people to drag.

H2.text: Why does rolling make heavy things so easy?

H3.text: On his way to college, Aarav's back tyre goes flat.

H4.text: Same level road, yet every push on the pedal feels like a hill. Why?

P2.text: When a body rolls over a surface, the force that opposes the rolling is rolling friction.

P3.text: A perfectly hard wheel on a perfectly hard floor touches at one point, and that point does not slide. No friction at all.

P5.text: But real wheels and floors squash a little where they meet. That squashing causes rolling friction.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. A fifty kilogram box on a rough floor.

S2.text: To keep it sliding steadily, Aarav pulls with one hundred and ninety six newtons. Exactly the kinetic friction.

S3.text: More load. Seventy five kilograms, two hundred and ninety four newtons. One hundred, three hundred and ninety two.

S4.text: Now the same box on a light trolley. The pull drops to just four point nine newtons.

S5.text: Add the same loads. At one hundred kilograms, only nine point eight.

S6.text: Both graph lines are straight: more load, more friction. But the rolling line is forty times flatter.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and look under one wheel.

S8.text: The floor and the tyre both squash. The wheel rests on a small patch, not a point.

S9.text: The floor pushes up from the front of that patch, so its push leans backwards. That backward part is rolling friction.

D1.text: Now the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. On a level floor, the normal force N equals m g.

D3.text: Step two. Sliding friction. f k equals mu k times N.

D4.text: Step three. Rolling friction has the same form: f r equals mu r times N. Mu r has no unit.

D5.text: Step four. Same load, same N. So f r over f k equals mu r over mu k.

D6.text: Step five. Mu r is far smaller than mu k. So rolling friction is far smaller.

T1.text: Remember this. For the same load, rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

R1.text: Now, back to Aarav's flat tyre. Link by link.

R2.text: A flat tyre squashes much more against the road.

R3.text: A bigger squash means a bigger mu r, so a bigger rolling friction.

R4.text: To keep the same speed, Aarav must push harder. That extra push is the hill he feels.

K1.text: Side by side. Sliding: the whole bottom of the box scrapes. Tiny bumps catch and tear.

K2.text: Rolling: each part of the wheel touches down and lifts straight off. Nothing scrapes. Only the squash is left.

K3.text: Now you try. A steel ball rolls on a soft carpet, and on a steel plate. Where is the rolling friction bigger? Pause and decide.

K4.text: On the carpet! The soft carpet squashes much more under the ball. More squash, more rolling friction.

V1.text: Friction is not always the enemy. Your foot pushes back on the ground, and friction pushes you forward.

V2.text: Your turn. On a perfectly frictionless road, could Aarav's bicycle start moving? Pause and decide.

V3.text: No! The back wheel would just spin. With no friction, the road cannot push the bicycle forward. Brakes need friction too.

V4.text: Where friction wastes energy, we cut it: oil, and ball bearings that turn sliding into rolling.

W2.text: A ten tonne wagon rolls on rails, with mu r of zero point zero zero two. Find the rolling friction. And if it skidded, with mu k of zero point four?

W3.text: N is ten thousand kilograms times nine point eight. Ninety eight thousand newtons.

W4.text: Rolling: zero point zero zero two times ninety eight thousand. One hundred and ninety six newtons.

W5.text: Skidding: zero point four times ninety eight thousand. Thirty nine thousand two hundred newtons.

W6.text: Two hundred times more. Ten tonnes on wheels needs the same pull as our fifty kilogram box sliding.

X2.text: Many students say rolling friction is zero, because the contact point does not slide.

X3.text: That is true only for a perfectly hard wheel. Real surfaces squash, so rolling friction is small, but never zero.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions comparing sliding and rolling friction.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A sixty kilogram crate slides on a floor, mu k zero point five. It is put on a twenty kilogram trolley, mu r zero point zero two. g is ten. By what factor does the steady pushing force fall? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Eighteen point seven five times.

A2.text: Sliding: N is six hundred newtons, so the force is three hundred.

A3.text: On the trolley, the load is eighty kilograms. N is eight hundred, so the force is sixteen.

A4.text: Three hundred over sixteen. Twenty five is the trap: it forgets the trolley.

Y2.text: One. Why does a flat tyre make cycling harder on the same road?

Y3.text: Two. Why is rolling friction not zero, if the contact point does not slide?

Y4.text: Three. How do ball bearings reduce friction in a machine?
